paragraphs: They entered the room almost at the same moment that the elder came in from his bedroom. Two monks of the hermitage were already in the cell, waiting for him. One was the Father Librarian, the other Father Païssy, a very learned man, so they said, and in poor health, though not old. There was also a tall young man, who looked about twenty-two, standing in the corner throughout the interview. He had a broad, fresh face and clever, observant, narrow brown eyes, and he wore ordinary clothes. He was a divinity student, living under the monastery’s protection. His expression was one of unquestioning but self-respecting reverence. Since he was in a subordinate and dependent position, and so not on an equal footing with the guests, he did not greet them with a bow.

Father Zossima was accompanied by a novice and by Alyosha. The two monks rose and greeted him with a very deep bow, touching the ground with their fingers, and then kissed his hand. The elder blessed them, then bowed to them just as deeply and asked for their blessing in return. The whole ceremony was performed very seriously and with an air of real feeling, not like an everyday rite. But Miüsov thought it was all done for deliberate effect. He stood in front of the other visitors. He ought, as he had reflected the evening before, to have gone up and received the elder’s blessing out of plain politeness, since it was the custom here, even if he did not kiss his hand. But when he saw all this bowing and kissing by the monks, he changed his mind at once. With dignified gravity he made a rather deep, conventional bow and moved away to a chair. Fyodor Pavlovitch did the same, mimicking Miüsov like an ape. Ivan bowed with great dignity and courtesy, but he too kept his hands at his sides, while Kalganov was so confused that he did not bow at all. The elder lowered the hand he had raised to bless them, bowed to them again, and asked them all to sit down. The blood rushed to Alyosha’s cheeks. He was ashamed. His fears were coming true.

Father Zossima sat down on a very old-fashioned mahogany sofa covered with leather. He had his visitors sit in a row along the opposite wall, on four mahogany chairs covered with shabby black leather. The monks sat, one by the door and the other by the window. The divinity student, the novice and Alyosha stayed standing. The cell was not very large and had a faded look. It held nothing but the most necessary furniture, coarse and poor in quality. There were two pots of flowers in the window and a number of holy pictures in the corner. A lamp was burning before one huge ancient ikon of the Virgin. Near it were two other holy pictures in shining frames, and next to them carved cherubs, china eggs, a Catholic ivory cross with a Mater Dolorosa embracing it, and several foreign engravings after the great Italian artists of past centuries. Beside these costly and artistic engravings hung several of the crudest Russian prints of saints and martyrs, of the kind sold for a few farthings at every fair. On the other walls were portraits of Russian bishops, past and present.

Miüsov took a quick glance at all these “conventional” surroundings and fixed an intent look on the elder. He had a high opinion of his own insight. That was a weakness excusable in him, since he was fifty, an age at which a clever man of the world with an established position can hardly help taking himself rather seriously. At first he did not like Zossima. There was indeed something in the elder’s face that many people besides Miüsov might not have liked. He was a short, bent little man with very weak legs. Though he was only sixty-five, he looked at least ten years older. His face was very thin and covered with a network of fine wrinkles, especially many around his eyes. The eyes were small, light-colored and quick, shining like two bright points. A sprinkling of gray hair showed at his temples. His pointed beard was small and scanty, and his lips, which smiled often, were as thin as two threads. His nose was not long, but sharp, like a bird’s beak.
“By all appearances, a malicious soul, full of petty pride,” thought Miüsov. He felt thoroughly dissatisfied with his position.
A cheap little clock on the wall hurriedly struck twelve, and that got the conversation started.

“Exactly on time,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch, “but no sign of my son Dmitri. I apologize for him, sacred elder!” (Alyosha shuddered all over at “sacred elder.”) “I’m always punctual myself, to the minute, remembering that punctuality is the courtesy of kings....”
“But you’re not a king, anyway,” Miüsov muttered, losing his self-control at once.

“Yes, that’s true. I’m not a king, and, would you believe it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, I knew that myself. But there! I always say the wrong thing. Your reverence,” he cried, with sudden pathos, “you see before you a buffoon in earnest! I introduce myself as such. It’s an old habit, alas! And if I sometimes talk nonsense out of place, it’s with an object, the object of amusing people and making myself agreeable. One must be agreeable, mustn’t one? Seven years ago I was in a little town where I had some business, and I made friends with some merchants there. We went to the captain of police, because we had to see him about something and ask him to dine with us. He was a tall, fat, fair, sulky man, the most dangerous type in such cases. It’s their liver. I walked straight up to him, with the ease of a man of the world, you know, and said, ‘Mr. Ispravnik, be our Napravnik.’ ‘What do you mean by Napravnik?’ said he. I saw in the first half-second that it had misfired. He stood there so glum. ‘I wanted to make a joke,’ said I, ‘for everyone’s entertainment, since Mr. Napravnik is our well-known Russian orchestra conductor, and what we need for the harmony of our undertaking is someone like that.’ And I explained my comparison very reasonably, didn’t I? ‘Excuse me,’ said he, ‘I am an Ispravnik, and I don’t allow puns on my calling.’ He turned and walked away. I followed him, shouting, ‘Yes, yes, you’re an Ispravnik, not a Napravnik.’ ‘No,’ he said, ‘since you called me a Napravnik, I am one.’ And would you believe it, it ruined our business! And I’m always like that, always like that. Always hurting myself with my politeness. Once, many years ago, I said to an influential person, ‘Your wife is a ticklish lady,’ meaning it in an honorable sense, about her moral qualities, so to speak. But he asked me, ‘Why, have you tickled her?’ I thought I’d be polite, so I couldn’t help saying, ‘Yes,’ and he gave me a fine tickling on the spot. Only that happened long ago, so I’m not ashamed to tell the story. I’m always hurting myself like that.”
“You’re doing it now,” muttered Miüsov, in disgust.
Father Zossima looked at them both in silence.

“Am I? Would you believe it, I knew that too, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, and let me tell you, I even foresaw I would, the moment I began to speak. And do you know, I foresaw too that you’d be the first to point it out. The minute I see my joke isn’t coming off, your reverence, both my cheeks feel as if they’re being dragged down to the lower jaw, and there’s almost a spasm in them. It’s been that way since I was young, when I had to make jokes for my living in noblemen’s houses. I’m an inveterate buffoon, and have been from birth, your reverence. It’s like a craze in me. I suppose it’s a devil inside me. But only a little one. A more serious one would have chosen another lodging. Though not your soul, Pyotr Alexandrovitch; you’re not a lodging worth having either. But I do believe—I believe in God, though I’ve had doubts lately. But now I sit and wait for words of wisdom. I’m like the philosopher Diderot, your reverence. Did you ever hear, most Holy Father, how Diderot went to see the Metropolitan Platon, in the time of the Empress Catherine? He walked in and said straight out, ‘There is no God.’ And the great bishop lifted his finger and answered, ‘The fool hath said in his heart there is no God.’ And Diderot fell down at his feet on the spot. ‘I believe,’ he cried, ‘and I will be christened.’ And so he was. Princess Dashkov was his godmother, and Potyomkin his godfather.”
“Fyodor Pavlovitch, this is unbearable! You know you’re telling lies and that stupid anecdote isn’t true. Why are you playing the fool?” cried Miüsov in a shaking voice.

“I’ve suspected all my life that it wasn’t true,” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried with conviction. “But I’ll tell you the whole truth, gentlemen. Great elder! Forgive me, the last part, about Diderot’s christening, I made up just now. I never thought of it before. I made it up to add some spice. I play the fool, Pyotr Alexandrovitch, to make myself agreeable. Though sometimes I really don’t know myself what I do it for. And as for Diderot, I heard the part up to ‘the fool hath said in his heart’ twenty times from the gentry around here when I was young. I heard your aunt tell the story, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. They all believe to this day that the infidel Diderot came to argue about God with the Metropolitan Platon....”
Miüsov got up, forgetting himself in his impatience. He was furious, and aware that he was making himself ridiculous.

What was happening in the cell was really incredible. For forty or fifty years, since the days of the earlier elders, no visitor had entered that cell without the deepest veneration. Almost everyone admitted to the cell felt that a great favor was being shown him. Many stayed on their knees for the whole visit. Many of those visitors had been men of high rank and learning, some even freethinkers who came out of curiosity. But all without exception had shown the deepest reverence and delicacy, for here there was no question of money, but only, on one side, love and kindness, and on the other, repentance and an eager desire to settle some spiritual problem or crisis. So this buffoonery amazed and bewildered the onlookers, or at least some of them. The monks, their faces unchanged, waited with earnest attention to hear what the elder would say, but seemed on the point of standing up, like Miüsov. Alyosha stood with his head hanging, on the verge of tears. What seemed strangest of all to him was that his brother Ivan, the only one on whom he had rested his hopes, and the only one with enough influence over their father to stop him, now sat quite unmoved, with downcast eyes, apparently waiting with interest to see how it would end, as though it had nothing to do with him. Alyosha did not dare to look at Rakitin, the divinity student, whom he knew almost intimately. He alone in the monastery knew what Rakitin was thinking.
